title: Binary search on the answer
sub: No array, but a monotonic answer: the “least x such that true” and “greatest x” templates, an O(n) check and the bounds
cards/0/body:
Koko Eating Bananas (LeetCode #875). There are piles of bananas piles and h hours. Each hour Koko picks one pile and eats up to k bananas from it; if the pile has fewer than k, she finishes it and rests for the rest of the hour. Find the minimum integer speed k at which she finishes within h hours. 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴, n ≤ h ≤ 10⁹, up to 10⁹ bananas per pile.

There is no array to search — but there are signals of binary search on the answer:

1. You are asked for the minimum or maximum value at which a condition holds.
2. For a fixed k the condition is easy to check: pile p takes ⌈p / k⌉ hours, the total takes O(n).
3. The answer is monotonic: if Koko makes it at speed k, she makes it at k + 1 too — no pile gets more hours.

Example: piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8. At k = 4 the hours are 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 — she makes it; at k = 3 it is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 — she does not. The answer is 4.
cards/1/q: The naive solution tries k = 1, 2, 3, … until the first speed that works. How many operations is that in the worst case?
cards/1/options/0: Up to 10⁹ speeds times 10⁴ piles — about 10¹³, too slow
cards/1/explain: With h = n the answer is the largest pile, up to 10⁹, and the scan goes all the way there. Each check walks over all piles — 10⁴ operations. That is 10¹³ in total: at the rule of thumb of 10⁸ operations per second, more than a day.
cards/1/wrong/1: 10⁴ is a single check of a single speed. There are up to 10⁹ candidate speeds.
cards/1/wrong/2: Checking one speed is not one operation: it sums the hours over all n piles.
cards/1/wrong/3: 3·10⁵ is exactly the optimal solution: about 30 checks of 10⁴ each. A sequential scan makes up to 10⁹ of them.
cards/2/title: The template: the least x such that true
cards/2/body:
Write down fits(k) = “finishes within h hours” for every k in a row: false, false, …, false, true, true, …. Monotonicity means there is exactly one switch. What we want is the first true: that is lower_bound, only not over an array but over a predicate on the range of possible answers.

The “least x such that true” template: lo is the smallest possible value, hi a value where true is guaranteed. Invariant: everything below lo is false, fits(hi) is true. While lo < hi: if fits(mid), the answer is not to the right of mid — hi = mid; otherwise it is to the right — lo = mid + 1. When lo == hi, that is the answer. For Koko lo = 1 and hi = max(piles): at that speed every pile takes one hour, n hours in total, and n ≤ h.

The cost: log₂ 10⁹ ≈ 30 checks of O(n) each — about 3·10⁵ operations instead of 10¹³. In general — O(log(range) · cost of the check).

In games this is how balancing tools tune a parameter against a monotonic check: the least damage at which the boss falls within N turns (the check is a combat simulation run), the smallest buffer that fits the peak frame of a recorded session.
cards/3/q: Build the Koko Eating Bananas solution.
cards/3/explain: The upper bound is the largest pile: there fits is guaranteed to be true. piles.Sum() also gives true, but the range is wider, and with 10⁴ piles of 10⁹ the sum does not fit in int — LINQ adds ints with overflow checking and throws OverflowException. The loop runs until lo == hi. “Within h” means hours <= h, exactly h hours is fine too. A k that works may be the answer, so hi = k, no − 1.
cards/4/task: The example from the problem: piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8. The rig will stop twice and ask which speed the code checks and which bound it moves.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: k = 6 worked, hi = 6. The candidates are [1..6]. What is the next check, and how does it end?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: mid = 1 + (6 − 1) / 2 = 3. At k = 3 the hours are ⌈3/3⌉ + ⌈6/3⌉ + ⌈7/3⌉ + ⌈11/3⌉ = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 — too slow. By monotonicity every speed below 3 is too slow as well: lo = k + 1 = 4. hi = 3 would throw away the answer: false says nothing about speeds above k.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: 8 is not less than 8 → lo = 5; answer 5
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: fits(4) == true — return 4 right away without narrowing
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: The candidates are [4..5]. At k = 4 it takes exactly 8 hours. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: The condition is finishing within h hours, i.e. hours <= h: exactly 8 is fine. hi = k = 4, the interval [4..4] has closed, the loop ends, the answer is 4. The template cannot and should not return “right away”: fits(k) == true does not yet prove that k is minimal — only the closed interval proves that.
cards/5/title: The second template: the greatest x such that true
cards/5/body:
Sometimes it is the other way round: you need the greatest x at which the condition holds, and the predicate goes true, …, true, false, …. An example is Sqrt(x) (LeetCode #69): the integer part of the square root, i.e. the largest r with r² ≤ x; 0 ≤ x ≤ 2³¹ − 1.

The mirror template with the invariant “fits(lo) is true, everything above hi is false”: if fits(mid), the answer is not to the left of mid — lo = mid; otherwise hi = mid − 1. And here is the trap: the middle must be rounded up. With two candidates, hi = lo + 1, the usual middle equals lo, and if fits(lo), then lo = mid — the same value: the interval does not shrink, and the loop runs forever.

The rule: the branch that assigns mid without ± 1 gets the middle from the other side: hi = mid goes with the lower middle, lo = mid with the upper one. The upper middle is lo + (hi − lo + 1) / 2, but with lo = 0, hi = int.MaxValue the parenthesis overflows; hi − (hi − lo) / 2 is safer.

The comparison overflows too: mid * mid does not fit in int once mid exceeds 46,340. Compute (long)mid * mid or compare mid <= x / mid.
cards/6/q: This MySqrt hangs forever on x = 8. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: lo = 0, hi = 8: mid = 4, 16 > 8 → hi = 3; mid = 1 → lo = 1; mid = 2, 4 ≤ 8 → lo = 2. Now lo = 2, hi = 3, the lower middle is 2, and lo = mid changes nothing. The lo = mid branch needs the upper middle: hi − (hi − lo) / 2.
cards/7/body:
Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (#1011): packages ship strictly in order; find the minimum capacity that gets everything shipped within D days. The check is greedy: load while it fits, otherwise start a new day; were D days enough? Bounds: lo = max(weights) — with less the heaviest package does not fit, hi = sum(weights) — everything in one day.
Split Array Largest Sum (#410): split an array of non-negative numbers into k contiguous parts so that the largest part sum is minimal — the same check “are k parts with sum ≤ x enough” and the same bounds.
Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets (#1482): search over the day, the check is a pass over the bloom days.
Magnetic Force Between Two Balls (#1552): place m balls at given positions so that the minimum distance is maximal. The check “is distance ≥ d possible”: put each next ball at the first position at least d away. If it works for d, it works for anything smaller — the maximum template.
Path With Minimum Effort (#1631, the pathfinding unit): the minimal largest height difference along a grid path — search over the difference with a grid traversal as the check.

The common signal: “minimise the maximum” or “maximise the minimum”, and checking a fixed answer is a greedy O(n) pass.
cards/8/q: Which problems are solved by binary search on the answer? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: The minimum capacity to ship packages in order within D days
cards/8/options/1: Split an array into k contiguous parts with the smallest possible largest sum
cards/8/options/2: Place m towers at given positions so that the minimum distance between them is maximal
cards/8/options/3: Check whether the array contains a duplicate
cards/8/options/4: Count how many times each word of a text occurs
cards/8/explain: The first three are “minimise the maximum” or “maximise the minimum” with a monotonic greedy check: #1011, #410 and #1552 from the previous card. Duplicates and word counts are not about finding a value: there is nothing to guess, you need one pass with a hash map.
cards/9/q: Magnetic Force Between Two Balls (#1552): find the largest d such that m balls can be placed at least d apart. Which binary search template?
cards/9/options/0: The greatest d such that true: fits(mid) → lo = mid, upper middle
cards/9/options/1: The least d such that true: fits(mid) → hi = mid, lower middle
cards/9/options/2: The greatest d: fits(mid) → lo = mid, lower middle as usual
cards/9/options/3: None: the “can be placed” predicate is not monotonic
cards/9/explain: If the balls fit with distance ≥ d, they fit with any smaller distance too: the predicate is true…true, false…false, and we need the last true. The lo = mid branch needs the upper middle — otherwise with hi = lo + 1 the loop hangs, just like MySqrt on x = 8.
cards/9/wrong/1: The first true here is d = 0 or 1: such a placement is always possible. We need the last true, not the first.
cards/9/wrong/2: The template is right, but the lower middle with hi = lo + 1 gives mid = lo, and lo = mid does not move the bound — an infinite loop.
cards/9/wrong/3: It is monotonic: a placement valid for d is valid for any smaller d — the distances are the same.
cards/10/q: You are solving Koko Eating Bananas out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: is the speed an integer? Is h ≥ n guaranteed? How large are the piles?
cards/10/items/1: Naive: try k from 1 upwards — up to 10⁹ speeds at O(n) each, about 10¹³ operations
cards/10/items/2: Idea: fits(k) is monotonic — binary search for the first true on [1, max(piles)]
cards/10/items/3: Code by the template: fits(mid) → hi = mid, otherwise lo = mid + 1; hours in long
cards/10/items/4: Run [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8: k = 6 yes, 3 no, 5 yes, 4 yes → answer 4
cards/10/items/5: Complexity: O(n log max) — about 30 passes over the array
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: h == n — the answer is max(piles), one pile, piles of 10⁹ and sum overflow
cards/10/explain: The key sentence of the explanation is the proof of monotonicity: “if she makes it at k, she makes it at k + 1”. Without it binary search is a guess, not a solution.
cards/11/title: When binary search on the answer is correct
cards/11/body:
The method rests on the monotonicity of the check, and you must prove it, not assume it. For Koko: ⌈p / k⌉ does not grow as k grows, so neither does the sum. Without monotonicity, when the answer “jumps”, binary search returns some switch point rather than the minimum.

The bounds are part of the proof too: fits(hi) must be true. Tighter bounds mean fewer iterations, but the gain is only logarithmic. For Koko you can raise the lower one — nobody finishes slower than ⌈sum / h⌉ bananas per hour — but that saves a few iterations out of 30.

A real-valued answer — a speed in m/s, a radius — is searched not with while (hi − lo > eps) but with a fixed number of iterations, say 100: the reason is under “Go deeper”.
cards/11/deep:
Real-valued answers. When the answer is not an integer (a speed in m/s, a radius), run a fixed number of iterations: 100 halvings shrink the range by 2¹⁰⁰ — more than a double can distinguish. The condition hi − lo > eps is riskier: for large values neighbouring doubles differ by more than eps, the middle rounds to one of the ends, and the loop never ends.

The cost of the check. The total is O(log(range) · cost of the check). If the check is a combat simulation or a level run, that is what is expensive: 30 runs instead of thousands. Binary search iterations are sequential — the next one depends on the result of the previous one — so it is the check itself that gets parallelised: for example, a thousand fights of one simulation spread across Jobs.

Path With Minimum Effort. The search over the difference with a grid traversal is O(E · log C), where C is the height range; Dijkstra with a maximum instead of a sum of weights is O(E log V). Both are accepted in interviews; we will cover the second one in the pathfinding unit.

The general idea. This is parametric search: an optimisation problem “find the best x” is turned into a decision problem “is x good enough”, and you search for the boundary. It works wherever checking is easier than optimising — and it is a common answer to “minimum of maximums”.
cards/12/q: Match the problem with its check and template.
